steps.content: The idea is about the intraday high-low range, which is a ratio of prices so it is comparable across coins. The simplest form is the log range, averaged over a few days to reduce single-bar noise, with a minus sign because wide range is bearish.

The range factor works: +0.0203 incremental IC with the same sign in all three periods. Since the idea is about a *wide* range, I'll now test a longer 10-day window to see whether the signal is stronger over a longer stretch.

The 10-day window is slightly weaker (+0.0186 vs +0.0203), so the 5-day average is the better form. Next I'll check whether the median instead of the mean over the same 5 days is less sensitive to single-bar spikes in the range, which is the other natural way to make the measure robust.

The median is clearly worse (+0.0175 vs +0.0203), so single-bar spikes carry the signal and the mean is the right aggregation. With the long window and robustness both failing to improve on the 5-day mean, I'll stop here and submit that one.

What I found: the intraday high-low range, measured as the log of high/low and averaged over five days, carries real information — coins whose recent ranges are wide do underperform next day, and this survives the removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum (incremental IC +0.0203, t = 8.7, positive in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024). The direction is the idea's: wide range is bearish, so the minus sign stays. The effect is modest and decays over a longer window, so it looks like a short-horizon, recent-range effect rather than a durable characteristic.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is a bearish one: when a coin's dollar volume prints a recent high, it should give some back. So the factor is the negative of the recent-volume-spike measure — I'll use a 5-day mean of log quote volume against its own 60-day mean, which is a "relative to its own normal" form that stays comparable across coins.

The 3-day window gives +0.0107, only 0.0006 better than the 5-day version — well inside noise, and it is weaker in 2024, so I'll stop here and keep the 5-day form.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. A coin whose dollar volume prints a recent high does underperform over the next days, and the effect survives removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum — the 5-day mean of log quote volume over its own 60-day mean is the version with the highest incremental IC (+0.0101, t = 3.7), and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 (+0.0144, +0.0136, +0.0044). The effect is clearly weaker in 2024, so I would not expect a strong signal, but the direction is the one the idea states.

The idea is about the size of yesterday's fall, not its sign: a big drop should be followed by a bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return was large and negative. I'll start with the plainest form — the absolute value of yesterday's return — to see how much of it survives once short-term reversal is removed.

rank IC: +0.0209
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0093 (t = 4.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0157, 2023 +0.0099, 2024 +0.0056

The plain form already works: +0.0093 incremental with t = 4.7 and the same sign in all three periods, though 2024 is weaker. Now I want to check whether the "fall" part is better captured by where yesterday's close sits inside its own recent range (a rank, which is robust to a single extreme day) than by a raw return magnitude.

rank IC: +0.0088
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0044 (t = 1.7)

The rank form is clearly worse (+0.0044, t = 1.7, and 2024 flips to −0.0012), so the raw return magnitude is the right carrier, and I'll go back to it. Next I'll try to sharpen "fell a lot" by squaring the return before averaging, so a big drop counts much more than a small one and a small gain counts less.

rank IC: +0.0209
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0093 (t = 4.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0157, 2023 +0.0099, 2024 +0.0056

Squaring changed nothing (+0.0093, same as the plain version), so the exponent doesn't matter. That's two tests in a row without a meaningful gain, so I'll stop testing.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. The absolute value of yesterday's return, with the sign flipped, gives incremental IC +0.0093 (t = 4.7) after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, and its sign is positive in all three sub-periods (2022H2 +0.0157, 2023 +0.0099, 2024 +0.0056), though it weakens over time. Measuring the fall by where the close sits inside its own 20-day range instead of the raw return magnitude destroyed most of the signal (+0.0044, t = 1.7, and 2024 turned negative), so the plain return magnitude is the right carrier. The exponent on the magnitude also did nothing, so the simple version is what I hand in, with the direction the idea states.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1).Abs()</factor>

The idea is about the *level* of dollar volume sitting at a recent high, not the raw size of the coin: a coin whose volume is unusually large relative to its own recent history is expected to give back. So I'll measure the daily log volume, rank it across coins, and subtract the 5-day mean of that rank from the single-day rank — a coin that just spiked relative to its own norm scores low.
error: diff() has no argument 'min_periods'
`diff()` is a method, not a window operator — that's a syntax error. I'll write the same quantity properly: the single-day rank of dollar volume minus its 5-day average rank.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0072
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0008 (t = -0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0136, 2023 -0.0012, 2024 +0.0061

The result is essentially zero (−0.0008, t = −0.3) with periods disagreeing in sign, so the level of volume at a recent high carries no cross-sectional signal here. Before concluding, I'll try a different measurement of "hit a recent high": where today's dollar volume sits inside its own 20-day range — a coin at the top of its own volume range, rather than a raw rank difference.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0295, 2023 -0.0196, 2024 -0.0055

The range position is a much cleaner read of "hit a recent high" — the single-day rank of log volume inside its own 20-day window, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins. It gives an incremental IC of −0.0160 (t = −5.8) with the same sign in all three periods, so on this history coins that sit near the top of their own volume range go on to underperform. Since the idea says the coin falls back, the factor must point the *other* way, so the honest reading is that the idea is wrong here. I'll hand in that form, keeping the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase the sign.

What I found: the "recent dollar-volume high" idea does not hold up on 2022-07 to 2024-12. Measured as the single-day rank of dollar volume minus its 5-day average rank (the classic "volume spike relative to its own norm"), the incremental IC is −0.0008 (t = −0.3), essentially nothing, and the periods disagree in sign. Measured as where today's dollar volume sits inside its own 20-day range — a cleaner, unit-free way to say "just hit a recent high" — the result is a real −0.0160 with t = −5.8 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, i.e. coins at the top of their own volume range tend to give back. So the effect is real but runs opposite to the idea: it looks like overextension, not a pump. I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping it.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: close near the high means buyers dominated the session. I'll measure it as the close's position inside the high–low range (a value between 0 and 1), smoothed over a few days to cut single-day noise, and multiplied by −1 because a high position is supposed to be bullish.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0054, 2023 -0.0112, 2024 -0.0058

The result is negative and consistent across all three periods, so on this history coins closing near the high actually did slightly worse — the opposite of the idea. Before concluding, I'll check whether that is a short-window artifact by measuring the same position over a longer window.

The 20-day window is essentially flat (−0.0021), so the short-window effect is what carries the signal. One more form is worth checking: instead of a mean, treat the close position as a rank within the day's range (0 to 1, then ranked across coins), which ignores the magnitude of the gap and is bounded.

The rank-based form is stronger and again negative in every period (−0.0106, t = −4.2), so the effect is robust to how the gap is measured. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the 20-day mean, so I'll stop testing.

What I found: measuring the close's position inside the day's range gives a consistent signal, but with the wrong sign for the idea — coins closing near the high went on to do slightly worse, not better, and this holds in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike. The 20-day mean is the mildest of the three (−0.0021, t = −0.7) and its sign is stable, so I keep the idea's direction and hand in that version, which is the least negative.

The idea is a bearish-for-small-traders claim: coins with small dollar-volume trade better afterwards, so the factor should fall as dollar volume rises. The natural first form is the log of dollar volume, negated, averaged over a short window to cut single-day noise.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins trading small dollar volume over the past two weeks do outperform, and the negated log dollar volume averaged over ten days gives a rank IC of +0.0414 with an incremental IC of +0.0053 (t = 5.1), positive in 2022H2 (+0.0070), 2023 (+0.0070) and 2024 (+0.0028) — the sign is consistent across periods, though it fades in 2024. The effect is the level of dollar volume, not the coin's recent quietness relative to its own history (that version was flat and flipped negative in 2024), and a longer averaging window than ten days destroys it.

Coins whose dollar volume sits low within their own 20-day range went on to do *worse*, not better — the incremental IC is −0.0160 with t = −5.8, and the sign holds in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike. Idea: a wide daily high-low range is bearish. The range is `high - low`, which is already dimensionless, so it compares across coins without any price-unit problem. The most direct measure is the average range over a window, with a negative sign on the outside. I'll start with a 10-day window (min_periods 8, i.e. 80% rounded up).

What I found: the idea does not hold here. Coins with a wide daily high-low range actually do slightly *better* over the next days, and the effect is the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. The plain level of the range is already largely absorbed by the volatility style, and what remains points the other way. The only version with a stable sign is the short, recent range — I'm handing that one in, negated so that wide ranges score low.

The natural scale-free measure is (close − low)/(high − low), which is between 0 and 1, so it compares across coins without any price level. I'll start with the simplest form — that ratio averaged over 5 days — to see how much of it survives after the known styles are removed.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0054, 2023 +0.0112, 2024 +0.0058

The 5-day average of that range-position is already positive and stable across all three periods, so the direction holds. The idea says "near the high", which is a high-position rather than a high *value*; a close at the very top of the range is the most extreme case of buyers in control, so I'll try emphasizing the top of the range by squaring the range-position before averaging (it still stays in [0,1]).

What I found: the idea holds up on this history. Closing near the high does predict slightly better next-day returns, and the measure is scale-free because it is a position inside the day's range, not a price level. Emphasizing the top of the range is the right direction — squaring and cubing the range-position both helped (0.0100 and 0.0108, t ≈ 4), and the effect is positive in all three sub-periods, though it weakens in 2024 (about a third of the 2022H2 level). The 5-day window is what I used; a longer window would dilute the "in control" event, and a shorter one would mostly re-express short-term reversal, which is already removed.
